Mongolia
Mongolia is a landlocked country in <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color>. It is bordered by <color=#3366CC>Russia</color> to the north and <color=#3366CC>China</color> to the south and covers
an area of 1564116 km2, making it the 18th-largest country in the world and the second largest landlocked nation after
<color=#3366CC>Kazakhstan</color>, as well as the largest landlocked country that does not border an <color=#3366CC>inland sea</color>. With a population of 3.5
million, Mongolia is the world's most sparsely populated sovereign state, excluding <color=#3366CC>Western Sahara</color>. The country
constitutes a significant portion of the <color=#3366CC>Mongolian Plateau</color>, and its natural environment is characterized by grassy
<color=#3366CC>steppe</color>, mountains to the north and west, and the <color=#3366CC>Gobi Desert</color> to the south. <color=#3366CC>Ulaanbaatar</color>, the capital and largest city, is
home to roughly half of the country's population.
The territory of modern-day Mongolia has been ruled by various nomadic empires, including the <color=#3366CC>Xiongnu</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Xianbei</color>,

the <color=#3366CC>Rouran</color>, the <color=#3366CC>First Turkic Khaganate</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Second Turkic Khaganate</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Uyghur Khaganate</color> and others. In 1206,
<color=#3366CC>Genghis Khan</color> founded the <color=#3366CC>Mongol Empire</color>, which became the largest contiguous land empire in history. His grandson
<color=#3366CC>Kublai Khan</color> conquered China proper and established the <color=#3366CC>Yuan dynasty</color>. After the collapse of the Yuan, the <color=#3366CC>Mongols</color>
retreated to Mongolia and resumed their earlier pattern of factional conflict, except during the era of <color=#3366CC>Dayan Khan</color> and
Tumen Zasagt Khan.
In the 16th century, Tibetan Buddhism spread to Mongolia. The <color=#3366CC>Qing dynasty</color> absorbed the country in the 17th century.
By the early 20th century, almost one-third of the adult male population were <color=#3366CC>Buddhist monks</color>. After the <color=#3366CC>collapse of the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Qing dynasty</color> in 1911, Mongolia declared independence and achieved actual independence from the Republic of China
in 1921. Shortly thereafter, the country became a satellite state of the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color>. In 1924, the Mongolian People's
Republic was founded as a socialist state. After the anti-communist <color=#3366CC>revolutions of 1989</color>, Mongolia conducted its own
peaceful democratic revolution in 1990. This led to a multi-party system, a new constitution of 1992, and transition to a
<color=#3366CC>market economy</color>.
Approximately 30% of the population is <color=#3366CC>nomadic</color> or semi-nomadic; horse culture remains integral. <color=#3366CC>Mahayana</color> Buddhism
is the majority religion (51.7%), with the irreligious being the second-largest group (40.6%). <color=#3366CC>Islam</color> is the third-largest
religious identification (3.2%), concentrated among ethnic Kazakhs. The vast majority of citizens are ethnic Mongols,
with roughly 5% of the population being Kazakhs, Tuvans, and other ethnic minorities, who are especially concentrated
in the western regions. Mongolia is a member of the <color=#3366CC>United Nations</color>, Asia Cooperation Dialogue, G77, Asian
Infrastructure Investment Bank, <color=#3366CC>Non-Aligned Movement</color> and a NATO global partner. Mongolia joined the <color=#3366CC>World Trade</color>
<color=#3366CC>Organization</color> in 1997 and seeks to expand its participation in regional economic and trade groups.
Etymology
The name Mongolia means the "Land of the Mongols" in Latin. The Mongolian word "Mongol" is of uncertain etymology.
Sükhbataar (1992) and de la Vaissière (2021) propose it is a derivation from Mugulü, the 4th-century founder of the
<color=#3366CC>Rouran Khaganate</color>, first attested as the 'Mungu', (<color=#3366CC>Chinese</color>:, Modern Chinese Měngwù, Middle Chinese Muwngu), a
branch of the Shiwei in an 8th-century <color=#3366CC>Tang dynasty</color> list of northern tribes, presumably related to the <color=#3366CC>Liao</color>-era Mungku
(<color=#3366CC>Modern Chinese</color> Měnggu, Middle Chinese MuwngkuX).
After the fall of the Liao dynasty in 1125, the Khamag Mongols became a leading tribe on the <color=#3366CC>Mongolian Plateau</color>.
However, their wars with the Jurchen-ruled <color=#3366CC>Jin dynasty</color> and the Tatar confederation had weakened them. The last head
of the tribe was Yesügei, whose son Temüjin (<color=#3366CC>Genghis Khan</color>) eventually united all the Shiwei tribes as the <color=#3366CC>Mongol</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color> (Yekhe Monggol Ulus). In the 13th century, the word Mongol grew into an umbrella term for a large group of
Mongolic-speaking tribes united under the rule of Genghis Khan.
Since the adoption of the Constitution of Mongolia in 1992, the official name of the state is "Mongolia" (Mongol Uls).
History
Prehistory and antiquity
The Khoit Tsenkher Cave in Khovd Province shows lively pink, brown, and red <color=#3366CC>ocher</color> paintings (dated to 20,000 years

ago) of <color=#3366CC>mammoths</color>, <color=#3366CC>lynx</color>, <color=#3366CC>bactrian camels</color>, and <color=#3366CC>ostriches</color>, earning it the nickname "the <color=#3366CC>Lascaux</color> of Mongolia". The Venus
figurines of Mal'ta (21,000 years ago) testify to the level of Upper <color=#3366CC>Paleolithic</color> art in northern Mongolia; Mal'ta is now part
of Russia. Neolithic agricultural settlements (c. 5500–3500 BC), such as those at Norovlin, Tamsagbulag, Bayanzag,
and Rashaan Khad, predate the introduction of horse-riding nomadism, a pivotal event in the history of Mongolia which
became the dominant culture. The ethnogenesis of Mongolic peoples is largely linked with the expansion of Ancient
Northeast Asians. The pastoralist lifestyle may in part be derived from the Western Steppe Herders but without much
geneflow between these two groups, suggesting cultural transmission.
Horse-riding nomadism has been documented during the Copper and Bronze Age Afanasevo culture (3500–2500 BC);
this <color=#3366CC>Indo-European</color> culture was active to the <color=#3366CC>Khangai Mountains</color> in central Mongolia. The wheeled vehicles found in the
burials of the Afanasevans have been dated to before 2200 BC. Pastoral nomadism and metalworking became more
developed with the Okunev culture (2nd millennium BC), <color=#3366CC>Andronovo culture</color> (2300–1000 BC) and Karasuk culture
(1500–300 BC), culminating with the Iron Age <color=#3366CC>Xiongnu</color> Empire in 209 BC. Monuments of the pre-Xiongnu Bronze Age
include deer stones, khirigsuur kurgans, square slab tombs, and rock paintings.
Although cultivation of crops has continued since the <color=#3366CC>Neolithic</color> period, agriculture has always remained small in scale
compared to pastoral nomadism. Agriculture may have first been introduced from the west or arose independently in
the region. The population during the Copper Age has been described as mongoloid in the east of what is now
Mongolia, and as europoid in the west. Tocharians (<color=#3366CC>Yuezhi</color>) and <color=#3366CC>Scythians</color> inhabited western Mongolia during the
Bronze Age. The mummy of a Scythian warrior, which is believed to be about 2,500 years old, was a 30- to 40-year-old
man with blond hair; it was found in the <color=#3366CC>Altai Mountains</color>. As equine nomadism was introduced, the political center of the
<color=#3366CC>Eurasian Steppe</color> shifted to Mongolia, where it remained until the 18th century. The intrusions of northern pastoralists
(e.g. the Guifang, Shanrong, and Donghu) into China during the <color=#3366CC>Shang dynasty</color> (1600–1046 BC) and <color=#3366CC>Zhou dynasty</color>
(1046–256 BC) presaged the age of nomadic empires.
Early states
Since prehistoric times, Mongolia has been inhabited by nomads who, from time to time, formed great confederations
that rose to power and prominence. Common institutions were the office of the Khan, the Kurultai (Supreme Council),
left and right wings, imperial army (Kheshig) and the decimal military system. The first of these empires, the Xiongnu of
undetermined ethnicity, were brought together by <color=#3366CC>Modu Shanyu</color> to form a confederation in 209 BC. They emerged as
the greatest threat to the <color=#3366CC>Qin dynasty</color>, forcing the latter to construct the <color=#3366CC>Great Wall of China</color>. It was guarded by up to
almost 300,000 soldiers during Marshal Meng Tian's tenure, as a means of defense against the destructive Xiongnu
raids. The vast Xiongnu empire (209 BC–93 AD) was followed by the Mongolic <color=#3366CC>Xianbei</color> empire (93–234), which also
ruled more than the entirety of present-day Mongolia. The <color=#3366CC>Rouran Khaganate</color> (330–555) of Xianbei provenance was
the first to use "Khagan" as an imperial title. It ruled a massive empire before being defeated by the <color=#3366CC>Göktürks</color>
(555–745), an even larger empire.
The Göktürks laid siege to Panticapaeum, present-day Kerch, in 576. They were succeeded by the <color=#3366CC>Uyghur Khaganate</color>
(745–840) who were defeated by the Kyrgyz. The Mongolic <color=#3366CC>Khitans</color>, descendants of the Xianbei, ruled Mongolia during
the Liao dynasty (907–1125), after which the Khamag Mongol (1125–1206) rose to prominence.
Lines 3–5 of the memorial inscription of Bilge Khagan (684–737) in central Mongolia summarizes the time of the
Khagans:
In battles they subdued the nations of all four sides of the world and suppressed them. They made those who had
heads bow their heads, and who had knees genuflect them. In the east up to the Kadyrkhan common people, in the
west up to the Iron Gate they conquered... These Khagans were wise. These Khagans were great. Their servants were
wise and great too. Officials were honest and direct with people. They ruled the nation this way. This way they held
sway over them. When they died ambassadors from Bokuli Cholug (Baekje Korea), Tabgach (Tang China), Tibet
(Tibetan Empire), <color=#3366CC>Avar</color> (Avar Khaganate), Rome (Byzantine Empire), Kirgiz, Uch-Kurykan, Otuz-Tatars, <color=#3366CC>Khitans</color>,
Tatabis came to the funerals. So many people came to mourn over the great Khagans. They were famous Khagans.
Mongol Empire to early 20th century
In the chaos of the late 12th century, a chieftain named Temüjin finally succeeded in uniting the Mongol tribes between
<color=#3366CC>Manchuria</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Altai Mountains</color>. In 1206, he took the title <color=#3366CC>Genghis Khan</color> and waged a series of military campaigns –
renowned for their brutality and ferocity – sweeping through much of Asia and forming the <color=#3366CC>Mongol Empire</color>, the largest
contiguous land empire in world history. Under his successors it stretched from present-day <color=#3366CC>Poland</color> in the west to
<color=#3366CC>Korea</color> in the east, and from parts of <color=#3366CC>Siberia</color> in the north to the Gulf of Oman and <color=#3366CC>Vietnam</color> in the south, covering some
33000000 km2, (22% of Earth's land area) and had a population of over 100 million people (about a quarter of Earth's
population at the time). The emergence of <color=#3366CC>Pax Mongolica</color> also significantly eased trade and commerce across Asia
during its height.
After Genghis Khan's death, the empire was subdivided into four kingdoms or Khanates. These eventually became
quasi-independent after the Toluid Civil War (1260–1264), which broke out in a battle for power following <color=#3366CC>Möngke</color>
<color=#3366CC>Khan</color>'s death in 1259. One of the khanates, the "Great Khaanate", consisting of the Mongol homeland and most of
modern-day China, became known as the Yuan dynasty under <color=#3366CC>Kublai Khan</color>, the grandson of Genghis Khan. He set up
his capital in present-day <color=#3366CC>Beijing</color>. After more than a century of power, the Yuan dynasty was overthrown by the <color=#3366CC>Ming</color>
<color=#3366CC>dynasty</color> in 1368, and the Yuan court fled to the north, thus becoming the <color=#3366CC>Northern Yuan</color> dynasty. As the Ming armies
pursued the Mongols into their homeland, they successfully sacked and destroyed the Mongol capital <color=#3366CC>Karakorum</color> and
other cities. Some of these attacks were repelled by the Mongols under Ayushridar and his general Köke Temür.
After the expulsion of the Yuan rulers from China proper, the Mongols continued to rule their homeland, known in
historiography as the Northern Yuan dynasty. With the division of the Mongol tribes, it was subsequently also known as
"The Forty and the Four" (Döčin dörben) among them. The next centuries were marked by violent power struggles
among various factions, notably the Genghisids and the non-Genghisid Oirats, as well as by several Ming invasions
(such as the five expeditions led by the Yongle Emperor).
In the early 16th century, <color=#3366CC>Dayan Khan</color> and his khatun Mandukhai reunited all Mongol groups under the Genghisids. In
the mid-16th century, <color=#3366CC>Altan Khan</color> of the Tümed, a grandson of Dayan Khan – but not a hereditary or legitimate khan –
became powerful. He founded <color=#3366CC>Hohhot</color> in 1557. After he met with the <color=#3366CC>Dalai Lama</color> in 1578, he ordered the introduction of
<color=#3366CC>Tibetan Buddhism</color> to Mongolia. (It was the second time this had occurred.) Abtai Khan of the Khalkha converted to
Buddhism and founded the Erdene Zuu Monastery in 1585. His grandson Zanabazar became the first Jebtsundamba
Khutughtu in 1640. Following the leaders, the entire Mongolian population embraced Buddhism. Each family kept
scriptures and Buddha statues on an altar at the north side of their <color=#3366CC>yurt</color>. Mongolian nobles donated land, money and
herders to the monasteries. As was typical in states with established religions, the top religious institutions, the
monasteries, wielded significant temporal power in addition to spiritual power.
The last khagan of the Northern Yuan was Ligden Khan in the early 17th century. He came into conflict with the
<color=#3366CC>Manchus</color> over the looting of Chinese cities and alienated most Mongol tribes. After his death in 1634, most <color=#3366CC>Inner</color>
<color=#3366CC>Mongolian</color> tribes had submitted to the Manchus by 1636, when they founded the Qing dynasty. The Khalkha followed in
1691, bringing all of present-day Mongolia under Manchu rule as the Northern Yuan Mongols, unable to resist the
Dzungars, also submitted in the late 17th century. After several Dzungar–Qing Wars, the Dzungars were virtually
annihilated during the Qing conquest of <color=#3366CC>Dzungaria</color> in 1755 and 1758.
Some scholars estimate that about 80% of the 600,000 or more <color=#3366CC>Dzungar were killed</color> by a combination of disease and
warfare. Outer Mongolia was given relative autonomy, being administered by the hereditary Genghisid khanates of
Tüsheet Khan, Sechen Khan, Zasagt Khan and Sain Noyon Khan. The Jebtsundamba Khutuktu had immense de facto
authority. The Manchu forbade mass Chinese immigration into the area, which allowed the Mongols to keep their
culture. The Oirats who migrated to the Volga steppes in Russia became known as Kalmyks. The main trade route
during this period was the Tea Road through Siberia; it had permanent stations located every 25 to 30 km, each of
which was staffed by 5–30 chosen families.
Until 1911, the Qing dynasty maintained control of Mongolia with a series of alliances and intermarriages, as well as
military and economic measures. Ambans (Manchu "high officials") were installed in <color=#3366CC>Khüree</color>, Uliastai, and Khovd, and
the country was divided into numerous <color=#3366CC>feudal</color> and ecclesiastical fiefdoms (which also placed people in power with
loyalty to the Qing). Over the course of the 19th century, the feudal lords attached more importance to representation
and less importance to the responsibilities towards their subjects. The behavior of Mongolia's nobility, together with
<color=#3366CC>usurious</color> practices by Chinese traders and the collection of imperial taxes in silver instead of animals, resulted in
widespread poverty among the nomads. By 1911 there were 700 monasteries in Outer Mongolia; their 115,000 monks
made up 21% of the population. Apart from the Jebtsundamba Khutuktu, there were 13 other reincarnating high lamas,
called 'seal-holding saints' (tamgatai khutuktu), in Outer Mongolia.
Modern history
With the <color=#3366CC>fall of the Qing dynasty</color> in 1911, Mongolia under the <color=#3366CC>Bogd Khaan</color> declared its independence. However, the
newly established <color=#3366CC>Republic of China</color> considered Mongolia to be part of its own territory. <color=#3366CC>Yuan Shikai</color>, the president of
the Republic of China, considered the republic to be the successor of the Qing. Bogd Khaan said that both Mongolia
and China had been administered by the Manchu during the Qing, and after the fall of the Qing dynasty the contract of
Mongolian submission to the Manchu had become invalid.
The area controlled by the Bogd Khaan was approximately that of the former Outer Mongolia during the Qing period. In
1919, after the <color=#3366CC>October Revolution</color> in Russia, Chinese troops led by warlord Xu Shuzheng occupied Mongolia. Warfare
erupted on the northern border. As a result of the <color=#3366CC>Russian Civil War</color>, the <color=#3366CC>White</color> Russian Lieutenant General Baron
Ungern led his troops into Mongolia in October 1920, defeating the Chinese forces in Niislel Khüree (now Ulaanbaatar)
in early February 1921 with Mongol support.
To eliminate the threat posed by Ungern, Bolshevik Russia decided to support the establishment of a communist
Mongolian government and army. This Mongolian army took the Mongolian part of Kyakhta from Chinese forces on 18
March 1921, and on 6 July Russian and Mongolian troops arrived in Khüree. Mongolia declared its independence again
on 11 July 1921. As a result, Mongolia was closely aligned with the Soviet Union over the next seven decades.
Mongolian People's Republic
In 1924, after the Bogd Khaan died, the country's political system was changed. The Mongolian People's Republic was
established. In 1928, <color=#3366CC>Khorloogiin Choibalsan</color> rose to power. The early leaders of the Mongolian People's Republic
included many with Pan-Mongolist ideals. However, changing global politics and increased Soviet pressure led to the
decline of Pan-Mongol aspirations in the following period.
<color=#3366CC>Khorloogiin Choibalsan</color> instituted collectivization of livestock, began the destruction of the Buddhist monasteries, and
carried out Stalinist purges, which resulted in the murders of numerous monks and other leaders. During the 1920s,
approximately one-third of the male population were monks. By the beginning of the 20th century, 750 monasteries
were functioning in Mongolia, and by the end of the 1930s almost all had been looted or razed.
In 1930, the Soviet Union stopped Buryat migration to the Mongolian People's Republic to prevent Mongolian
reunification. All leaders of Mongolia who did not fulfill Stalin's demands to perform Red Terror against Mongolians
were executed, including Peljidiin Genden and Anandyn Amar. The <color=#3366CC>Stalinist purges in Mongolia</color>, which began in 1937,
killed more than 30,000 people. Under Stalinist influence, an estimated 17,000 monks were killed. Choibalsan died
suspiciously in the Soviet Union in 1952. <color=#3366CC>Comintern</color> leader Bohumír Šmeral said, "People of Mongolia are not
important, the land is important. Mongolian land is larger than England, France and Germany".
After the <color=#3366CC>Japanese invasion of neighboring Manchuria</color> in 1931, Mongolia was threatened on this front. During the
Soviet-Japanese Border War of 1939, the Soviet Union successfully defended Mongolia against Japanese
expansionism. Mongolia fought against Japan during the Battles of Khalkhin Gol in 1939 and during the
<color=#3366CC>Soviet–Japanese War</color> in August 1945 to liberate Inner Mongolia from Japan and Mengjiang.
Cold War
The February 1945 <color=#3366CC>Yalta Conference</color> provided for the Soviet Union's participation in the <color=#3366CC>Pacific War</color>. One of the Soviet
conditions for its participation, put forward at Yalta, was that after the war Outer Mongolia would retain its
independence. The referendum took place on 20 October 1945, with (according to official numbers) 100% of the
electorate voting for independence.
After the establishment of the <color=#3366CC>People's Republic of China</color>, both countries confirmed their mutual recognition on 6
October 1949. However, the Republic of China (ROC), which still held a seat on the <color=#3366CC>United Nations Security Council</color>
despite its defeat in the <color=#3366CC>Chinese Civil War</color>, used its Security Council veto in 1955 to stop the admission of the
Mongolian People's Republic to the United Nations on the grounds it recognized all of Mongolia—including Outer
Mongolia—as part of China. This was the only time the ROC ever used its veto. Hence, and because of the repeated
threats to veto by the ROC, Mongolia did not join the UN until 1961 when the Soviet Union agreed to lift its veto on the
admission of <color=#3366CC>Mauritania</color> (and any other newly independent African state), in return for the admission of Mongolia.
Faced with pressure from nearly all the other African countries, the ROC relented under protest. Mongolia and
Mauritania were both admitted to the UN on 27 October 1961.
On 26 January 1952, <color=#3366CC>Yumjaagiin Tsedenbal</color> took power after the death of Choibalsan. Tsedenbal was the leading
political figure for more than 30 years. While Tsedenbal was visiting Moscow in August 1984, his severe illness
prompted the parliament to announce his retirement and replaced him with Jambyn Batmönkh.
Post-Cold War
The <color=#3366CC>dissolution of the Soviet Union</color> in 1991 strongly influenced Mongolian politics and youth. Its people undertook the
peaceful Democratic Revolution in <color=#3366CC>January 1990</color> and the introduction of a multi-party system and a market economy.
At the same time, the transformation of the former <color=#3366CC>Marxist-Leninist</color> Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party to the
current social democratic Mongolian People's Party reshaped the country's political landscape.
A new constitution was introduced in 1992, and the term "People's Republic" was dropped from the name. The
transition to a market economy was often rocky; during the early 1990s the country had to deal with high inflation and
food shortages. The first election victories for non-communist parties came in 1993 (presidential elections) and 1996
(parliamentary elections). China has supported Mongolia's application for membership in the Asia Cooperation
Dialogue, <color=#3366CC>Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation</color> and granting it observer status in the <color=#3366CC>Shanghai Cooperation</color>
<color=#3366CC>Organisation</color>.
Geography
At 1564116 km2, Mongolia is the world's 18th-largest country. It mostly lies between latitudes 41° and 52°N (a small
area is north of 52°), and longitudes 87° and 120°E. The geography is varied, with the <color=#3366CC>Gobi Desert</color> to the south and
cold, mountainous regions to the north and west. Much of the land consists of the Mongolian–Manchurian grassland,
with forested areas accounting for 11.2% of the total land area. The whole of Mongolia is considered to be part of the
<color=#3366CC>Mongolian Plateau</color>. The highest point is Khüiten Peak in the Tavan Bogd massif in the far west at 4374 m. The basin of
Uvs Lake, shared with <color=#3366CC>Tuva Republic</color> in Russia, is a natural <color=#3366CC>World Heritage Site</color>.
Climate
Mongolia is high, cold and windy. It has an extreme continental climate with long, cold winters and short summers,
during which most of its annual precipitation falls. Most of the country is hot in the summer and extremely cold in the
winter, with January averages dropping as low as -30 °C. In winter the region comes under the influence of the Siberian
Anticyclone. A vast front of cold, heavy, shallow air comes in from <color=#3366CC>Siberia</color> in winter and collects in river valleys and low
basins, causing very cold temperatures, while slopes of mountains are much warmer due to the effects of temperature
inversion (temperature increases with altitude). The annual average temperature in Ulaanbaatar is 1.3 °C, making it the
world's coldest capital city. The country is subject to occasional harsh climatic conditions known as zud, in which large
proportions of livestock die from starvation or freezing temperatures or both, resulting in economic upheaval for the
largely pastoral population.
A unique microclimate is the fertile grassland-forest region of central and eastern Arkhangai Province and northern
Ovorkhangai Province where January temperatures are on average the same and often higher than the warmest desert
regions to the south in addition to being more stable. The <color=#3366CC>Khangai Mountains</color> play a role in forming this microclimate. In
Tsetserleg, the warmest town in this microclimate, nighttime January temperatures rarely go under -30 °C while
daytime January temperatures often reach 0 °C to 5 °C. Mongolia is known as the "Land of the Eternal Blue Sky" or
"Country of Blue Sky" (Mongolian: "Mönkh khökh tengeriin oron") because it has over 250 sunny days per year.
Precipitation is highest in the north (average of 200 to 350 mm per year) and lowest in the south, which receives 100 to
200 mm annually. The sparsely populated far north of Bulgan Province averages 600 mm in annual precipitation. The
highest annual precipitation of 622 mm occurred in the forests of Bulgan Province, and the lowest of 42 mm occurred in
the Gobi Desert.
Environmental issues
Wildlife
The name "Gobi" is a Mongol term for a desert steppe, which usually refers to a category of arid rangeland with
insufficient vegetation to support <color=#3366CC>marmots</color> but with enough to support camels. Mongols distinguish Gobi from desert
proper, although the distinction is not always apparent to outsiders unfamiliar with the Mongolian landscape.
Gobi rangelands are fragile and easily destroyed by overgrazing, which results in expansion of the true desert, a stony
waste where not even <color=#3366CC>Bactrian camels</color> can survive. The arid conditions in the Gobi are attributed to the <color=#3366CC>rain shadow</color>
<color=#3366CC>effect</color> caused by the Himalayas. Before the Himalayas were formed by the collision of the Indo-Australian plate with the
Eurasian plate 10 million years ago, Mongolia was a flourishing habitat for major fauna but still somewhat arid and cold
due to distance from sources of evaporation. Sea turtle and mollusk fossils have been found in the Gobi, apart from
well-known dinosaur fossils. <color=#3366CC>Tadpole shrimps</color> are still found in the Gobi today. The eastern part of Mongolia including
the Onon and Kherlen rivers and Lake Buir form part of the <color=#3366CC>Amur river</color> basin draining to the Pacific Ocean. It hosts
some unique species like the Eastern brook lamprey, Daurian crayfish (cambaroides dauricus) and Daurian pearl
oyster (dahurinaia dahurica) in the Onon/Kherlen rivers as well as Siberian prawn (exopalaemon modestus) in Lake

Buir. Many large mammals inhabit the nation including <color=#3366CC>saiga</color>, argali, Siberian ibex, <color=#3366CC>elk</color>, Altai wapiti, <color=#3366CC>reindeer</color>, <color=#3366CC>wild boar</color>,
<color=#3366CC>onager</color>, wild horse, <color=#3366CC>snow leopard</color>, Mongolian wolf, and <color=#3366CC>brown bear</color>. A few large mammals have also been extirpated
from the nation including Ussuri dhole, <color=#3366CC>tiger</color>, and <color=#3366CC>European bison</color>.
Government and politics
Mongolia is a <color=#3366CC>semi-presidential</color> <color=#3366CC>representative democratic</color> <color=#3366CC>republic</color> with a directly-elected president. The people also
elect the deputies in the unicameral legislature, the State Great Khural. The president appoints the prime minister and
nominates the cabinet on the proposal of the prime minister. The prime minister is the head of the executive branch.
The State Great Khural, with 126 seats, is chaired by the chairman of the State Great Khural. Its members are directly
elected, every four years, by popular vote. According to V-Dem Democracy Indices, Mongolia was autocratizing in
The president is able to veto the laws made by parliament, appoint judges and court justices, and appoint
ambassadors. The parliament can override that veto by a two-thirds majority vote. The constitution provides three
requirements for taking office as president: the candidate must be a native-born Mongolian, be at least 45 years old,
and have resided in Mongolia for five years before taking office. The president must also suspend their party
membership. In June 2021, former Prime Minister Ukhnaagiin Khürelsükh, the candidate of the ruling Mongolian
People's Party, became the country's sixth democratically elected president after winning the presidential election. The
largest political parties are the Mongolian People's Party (MPP) and the Democratic Party. The non-governmental
organization Freedom House considers Mongolia to be free. The Mongolian People's Party – known as the Mongolian
People's Revolutionary Party (MPRP) between 1924 and 2010 – governed the country from 1921 to 1996 (in a
<color=#3366CC>one-party system</color> until 1990). The party was out of power for the first time in the 1996 parliamentary elections, when the
opposition Democratic Union Coalition held the majority for four years. However, after many political crises and
unpopularity, the coalition lost much of its seats to the MPRP in the 2000 election. Subsequently, the Democratic Party
was founded in 2000 through the merger of five parties and became the primary opposition to the MPRP up until the
2004 elections, when it became an almost-equal coalition partner to the MPRP. The Democratic Party became the
dominant political force between 2012 to 2016, when it held the presidency, prime ministership, and speakership. The
MPP won a landslide victory in the 2016 election and again in the 2020 election. Electoral reforms in 2023 allowed
minor parties to be more represented in parliament via proportional representation. Consequently, the MPP's
supermajority was reduced to a slim majority in the 2024 elections, allowing the Democratic Party and three other
parties to make up almost half of the expanded State Great Khural. Since 2024, there have been three prime ministers
and three different coalition governments led by the MPP. The current prime minister is Nyam-Osoryn Uchral, who has
served since March 2026.

Foreign relations
Mongolia maintains many many diplomatic missions and embassies in other countries. Foreign relations traditionally
focus on its two large neighbors, Russia and China. Mongolia is economically dependent on these countries: China is
its largest export partner at a 78% share, far above the other top countries (Switzerland at 15%; Singapore 3%).
Mongolia receives 36% of imports from China and 29% from Russia. Mongolia is pursuing a trilateral partnership with
China and Russia through the Power of Siberia 2 natural gas pipeline, with a contract to be signed in the "near future"
according to Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak. Due to China's status as Mongolia's most important
trading partner, Mongolia has been trying to stay out of the current US-China confrontation.
Mongolia has been a member of the Forum of Small States since its founding in 1992. It has begun seeking positive
relations with a wider range of other countries especially in cultural and economic matters, focusing on encouraging
foreign direct investment and trade. Mongolia has been pursuing a third neighbor policy since early 1990s to build
deeper relations and partnerships with countries beyond its two surrounding neighbors. US Vice President <color=#3366CC>Joe Biden</color>
visited Mongolia in 2011, supporting third neighbor policy.
Mongolia supported the <color=#3366CC>2003 invasion of Iraq</color> and has sent several successive contingents of 103 to 180 Mongolian
troops each to <color=#3366CC>Iraq</color>. About 130 troops were deployed to <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color>. 200 Mongolian troops served in <color=#3366CC>Sierra Leone</color> on a
UN mandate to protect the UN's special court set up there, and in July 2009, Mongolia sent a battalion to <color=#3366CC>Chad</color> in
support of MINURCAT.
From 2005 to 2006, about 40 troops were deployed with the Belgian and Luxembourg contingents in <color=#3366CC>Kosovo</color>. On 21
November 2005, <color=#3366CC>George W. Bush</color> became the first-ever sitting US president to visit Mongolia. In 2004, under Bulgarian
chairmanship, the <color=#3366CC>Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe</color> invited Mongolia as its newest Asian partner.
Legal system
The judiciary of Mongolia is made up of a three-tiered court system: first instance courts in each provincial district and
each <color=#3366CC>Ulaanbaatar district</color>; appellate courts for each province and also the Capital Ulaanbaatar; and the court of last
resort (for non-constitutional matters) at the Supreme Court of Mongolia. For questions of constitutional law, there is a
separate constitutional court. Arbitration centers provide <color=#3366CC>alternative dispute resolution</color> options for commercial and other
disputes.
A Judicial General Council nominates judges, who must then be confirmed by the parliament and appointed by the
president.
Economy
Economic activity in Mongolia has long been based on herding and agriculture, although development of extensive
mineral deposits of copper, coal, molybdenum, tin, tungsten and gold have emerged as a driver of industrial production.
Besides mining (21.8% of GDP) and agriculture (16% of GDP), dominant industries in the composition of GDP are
wholesale and retail trade and service, transportation and storage, and real estate activities. Also, Mongolia produces
one-fifth of the world's raw <color=#3366CC>cashmere</color>. The <color=#3366CC>informal economy</color> is estimated to be at least one-third the size of the official
economy. As of 2022, 78% of exports went to the <color=#3366CC>PRC</color>, and the PRC supplied 36% of Mongolia's imports.
According to the <color=#3366CC>Asian Development Bank</color>, 27.1% of the population lived below the national poverty line in 2022, and
GDP per capita was estimated at $12,100. Real GDP grew by 7% in 2023 as a result of record-high coal production,
driven by strong demand from China. Despite a robust increase in import volumes, Mongolia recorded a current
account surplus from the sharp increase in coal exports. Lower global food and fuel prices resulted in a 7% drop in
inflation in early 2024. Mining sector growth is expected to continue driving GDP growth, although the <color=#3366CC>International</color>
<color=#3366CC>Monetary Fund</color> predicts the current account balance will revert to a sizable deficit because of declining coal prices.
The <color=#3366CC>World Bank</color> has stated that expansion of mining and large public investment provide a positive outlook for
development prospects, although challenges remain from inflation, weaker external demand from China, and persistent
fiscal risks due to sizable contingent liabilities. In 2011, Citigroup analysts determined Mongolia to be one of the "global
growth generating" countries, which are countries with the most promising growth prospects for 2010–2050. The
Mongolian Stock Exchange, established in 1991 in Ulaanbaatar, is among the world's smallest stock exchanges by
<color=#3366CC>market capitalization</color>. As of 2024, it has 180 companies listed with a total market capitalization of US$3.2 billion. The
<color=#3366CC>International Finance Corporation</color> currently ranks Mongolia as 81st globally in its ease of doing business scoring.
Mongolia was ranked 78th in the Global Innovation Index in 2025.
Mineral industry
Minerals represent more than 80% of Mongolia's exports, a proportion expected to rise to 95%. Fiscal revenues from
mining represented 21% of government income in 2010 and rose to 24% in 2018. About 3,000 mining licenses have
been issued. Mining continues to rise as a major industry as evidenced by the number of Chinese, Russian and
Canadian firms starting mining businesses.
In 2009 the government negotiated an agreement with <color=#3366CC>Rio Tinto</color> and Ivanhoe Mines to develop the Oyu Tolgoi copper
and gold deposit, the largest foreign investment project in Mongolia at the time. The mine is a major producer of copper
and gold, with plans to further develop underground production and reach an output of 500,000 tons of copper per year.
Gold production in 2015 was 15 metric tons. Lawmakers have attempted to finance the development of the Tavan
Tolgoi area, the world's largest untapped coal deposit with more than six billion tonnes of coal reserves. However,
proposed international partnerships failed in 2011 and 2015, with Mongolia further canceling an international <color=#3366CC>initial</color>
<color=#3366CC>public offering</color> in 2020, citing financial and political difficulties. In September 2022, Mongolia built and launched a
233-km direct rail link to China, which is a milestone in Mongolia's plan to become China's leading supplier of coal from
Tavan Tolgoi.

Communications
Postal services are provided by state-owned Mongol Post and 54 other licensed operators.
Energy
Mongolia imports 98% of its fuel and is building its first ever oil refinery to reduce its foreign energy dependency.
Transportation
The <color=#3366CC>Trans-Mongolian Railway</color> is the main rail link between Mongolia and its neighbors. It begins at the <color=#3366CC>Trans-Siberian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Railway</color> in Russia at <color=#3366CC>Ulan-Ude</color>, crosses into Mongolia, runs through Ulaanbaatar, then passes into China at Erenhot
where it joins the Chinese railway system. A separate railroad link connects Choibalsan with the Trans-Siberian
Railway. However, that link is closed to passengers after Chuluunkhoroot. Mongolia also has a 233 km-long cargo rail
link from the Tavan Tolgoi coal mine to Chinese border.
The main international airport is Chinggis Khaan International Airport, located approximately 52 km south of
Ulaanbaatar. Direct flights exist to South Korea, mainland China, Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Russia, Germany, and
Turkey. MIAT Mongolian Airlines is the national air carrier, operating international flights, while air carriers such as Aero
Mongolia and Hunnu Airlines serve domestic and short international routes.
Many overland roads are unimproved. There are paved roads from Ulaanbaatar to the Russian and Chinese borders,
from Ulaanbaatar east- and westward (the so-called Millennium Road), and from Darkhan to Bulgan. Mongolia has
4800 km of paved roads, with 1800 km of that total completed in 2013 alone.
Demographics
In 2024 the population was 3,544,835, per the National Statistics Office of Mongolia. This figure includes the total
number of citizens who usually reside in Mongolia (for more than 183 days or six months), as well as citizens living
abroad. 51% of the population was female and 49% male, with 71.2% residing in urban areas, compared to 21.8% in
rural areas. The population growth rate was estimated at 1.2% in 2007.
The first census in the 20th century was carried out in 1918 and recorded a population of 647,500. Since the end of
socialism, Mongolia has experienced a decline of total fertility rate (children per woman) that is steeper than in any
other country in the world, according to recent UN estimations: in 1970–1975, fertility was estimated to be 7.33 children
per woman, dropping to about 2.1 in 2000–2005. The decline ended and in 2005–2010, the fertility value increased to
2.8 in 2013 and stabilized afterwards at a rate of about 2.5-2.6 children per woman around 2020.
The Mongols are moderately homogeneous; ethnic Mongols account for about 95% of the population and consist of
Khalkha and other groups, all distinguished primarily by dialects of the Mongol language. The Khalkha make up 86% of
the ethnic Mongol population. The remaining 14% include Oirats, Buryats and others. <color=#3366CC>Turkic peoples</color> (Kazakhs and
Tuvans) constitute 4.5% of Mongolia's population, and the rest are Russian, Chinese, Korean and American
nationalities.
Major cities
As of 2020, 47.6% of the population lives in Ulaanbaatar, further 21.4% lived in Darkhan, <color=#3366CC>Erdenet</color>, the aimag centers
and sum centers, and other permanent settlements, and 31.0% in rural areas.
• Under Ulaanbaatar administration
Languages
The official and national language is <color=#3366CC>Mongolian</color>. A member of the Mongolic language family, the standard dialect is
Khalkha Mongol. It coexists with various other, largely mutually intelligible varieties of Mongolic such as Oirat, Buryat,
and Khamnigan. Several dialects have been morphing to become more like the central Khalkha dialect in recent years.
Most speakers of these dialects are located in the western part of the country, namely Bayan-Ölgii, Uvs, and Khovd.
<color=#3366CC>Kazakh</color>, a <color=#3366CC>Turkic language</color>, is the majority language in Bayan-Ölgii, while Tuvan is another Turkic language spoken in
Khövsgöl. Mongolian Sign Language is the principal language of the deaf community.
As of the mid-2020s, Mongolian is mainly written using the Mongolian Cyrillic alphabet, introduced during the 1940s.
Since the 1990 revolution there has been a minor revival of the historic <color=#3366CC>Mongolian script</color>, which is still the official script
used by Mongols in neighboring Inner Mongolia. Although Mongolian script has officially been declared the national
script, and is taught from the sixth grade onward at schools, it remains mostly confined to ceremonial usage in daily life.
In 2025, Mongolia began using both the Cyrillic and traditional Mongolian scripts for legal papers and official
documents.
Since 1990, English has quickly supplanted Russian as the most popular foreign language. In the communist era,
Russian was a vital language for mobility and professional communication, with a large number of students studying in
the Soviet Union as well as a large number of Soviet professionals and soldiers located within Mongolia. Since then,
the education system has oriented away from the Soviet Union to the West, and English has become the dominant
foreign language, aided by liberalized media, international aid agencies, the rise of private education and tutoring, as
well as official government policy. In the 2014–2015 academic year, 59% of the overall student population studied
English at public secondary schools. In 2023, English was declared the "first foreign language", and to be taught from
the third grade.
As of the 2014–2015 academic year, the most popular foreign language in specialized language courses were (ordered
by popularity), English, <color=#3366CC>Chinese</color>, Russian, <color=#3366CC>Japanese</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Korean</color>. Korean in particular has gained popularity as tens of
thousands of Mongolians work in South Korea, forming the largest group of Mongolians abroad.
Religion
According to the 2020 National Census, among Mongolians aged 15 and above, 51.7% were Buddhists, while 40.6%
were <color=#3366CC>non-religious</color>. Mongolian shamanism has been widely practiced throughout the history of what is now Mongolia,
with similar beliefs being common among the nomads of central Asia. This gradually gave way to <color=#3366CC>Tibetan Buddhism</color>,
but shamanism has left a mark on religious culture, and it continues to be practiced. The Kazakhs of western Mongolia,
some Mongols, and other Turkic peoples in the country traditionally adhere to Islam.
Throughout much of the 20th century, the communist government repressed religious practices. It targeted the clergy of
the Mongolian Buddhist Church, which had been tightly intertwined with the previous feudal government structures (e.g.
from 1911 on, the head of the church had also been the khan). In the late 1930s, the regime under Choibalsan closed
almost all of Mongolia's over 700 Buddhist monasteries and killed at least 30,000 people, of whom 18,000 were lamas.
The number of Buddhist monks dropped from 100,000 in 1924 to 110 in 1990.
The <color=#3366CC>fall of communism</color> in 1991 restored public religious practice. Tibetan Buddhism, which had been the predominant
religion prior to the rise of communism, again rose to become the most widely practiced religion in Mongolia.
The end of religious repression in the 1990s also allowed for other religions to spread in the country. According to the
Christian missionary group Barnabas Fund, the number of Christians grew from just four in 1989 to around 40,000 as of
2008. In May 2013, <color=#3366CC>The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints</color> held a cultural program to celebrate 20 years in
Mongolia, with 10,900 members and 16 church buildings. There are some 1,000 Catholics, and in 2003 a missionary
from the <color=#3366CC>Philippines</color> was named Mongolia's first <color=#3366CC>Catholic</color> bishop. In 2017 <color=#3366CC>Seventh-day Adventists</color> reported 2,700
members in six churches up from zero members in 1991.
Education
During the state socialist period, education was one of the areas of significant achievement. Before the People's
Republic, literacy rates were below one percent. By 1952, illiteracy was virtually eliminated, in part through the use of
seasonal boarding schools for children of nomadic families. Funding to these boarding schools was cut in the 1990s,
contributing to slightly increased illiteracy. Primary and secondary education 12 years. English is taught in all secondary
schools across Mongolia, beginning in fourth grade.
Mongolian national universities are all spin-offs from the National University of Mongolia and the Mongolian University
of Science and Technology. Almost three in five youths enroll in university. There was a six-fold increase in students
between 1993 and 2010.

Culture
The Soyombo symbol represents the sun, moon, stars, and heavens per standard cosmological symbology abstracted
from that seen in traditional thangka paintings.
Architecture
The traditional dwelling is known as a ger. In the past it was known by the Turkic term <color=#3366CC>yurt</color>, but this has been changing
as the Mongolian term becomes better known in English-speaking countries. According to Mongolian artist and art critic
N. Chultem, the ger was the basis for development of traditional Mongolian architecture. In the 16th and 17th centuries,
lamaseries were built throughout the country. Many of them started as ger-temples. When they needed to be enlarged
to accommodate the growing number of worshippers, the Mongolian architects used structures with 6 and 12 angles
with pyramidal roofs to approximate to the round shape of a ger. Further enlargement led to a quadratic shape of the
temples. The roofs were made in the shape of marquées. The trellis walls, roof poles and layers of felt were replaced
by stone, brick, beams and planks, and became permanent.
Chultem distinguishes three styles in traditional Mongolian architecture: Mongolian, Tibetan and <color=#3366CC>Chinese</color> as well as
combinations of the three. Among the first quadratic temples was Batu-Tsagaan (1654) designed by Zanabazar. An
example of the ger-style architecture is the lamasery Dashi-Choiling in Ulaanbaatar. The temple Lavrin (18th century) in
the Erdene Zuu lamasery was built in the Tibetan tradition. An example of a temple built in the Chinese tradition is the
lamasery Choijing Lamiin Sume (1904), which is a museum today. The quadratic temple Tsogchin in lamasery Gandan
in Ulaanbaatar is a combination of the Mongolian and Chinese tradition. The temple of Maitreya (disassembled in 1938)
is an example of the Tibeto-Mongolian architecture. Dashi-Choiling monastery has commenced a project to restore the
temple and the 25 m sculpture of <color=#3366CC>Maitreya</color>.
Visual arts
Before the 20th century, most works of the fine arts had a religious function, and therefore Mongolian fine arts were
heavily influenced by religious texts. Thangkas were usually painted or made in appliqué technique. Bronze sculptures
usually showed Buddhist deities. A number of great works are attributed to Zanabazar.
In the late 19th century, painters like "Marzan" Sharav turned to more realistic painting styles. Under the Mongolian
People's Republic, <color=#3366CC>socialist realism</color> was the dominant painting style, however traditional thangka-like paintings dealing
with secular, nationalist themes were also popular, a genre known as "Mongol zurag". Among the first attempts to
introduce <color=#3366CC>modernism</color> was the painting Ehiin setgel (Mother's love) created by Tsevegjav in the 1960s. The artist was
purged as his work was censored. All forms of fine arts flourished only after <color=#3366CC>perestroika</color> in the late 1980s. Otgonbayar
Ershuu is arguably one of the most well-known modern artists in the Western world; he is portrayed in the film
"ZURAG" by Tobias Wulff.
Music
The music of Mongolia is strongly influenced by nature, nomadism, shamanism, and Tibetan Buddhism. The traditional
music includes a variety of instruments, famously the morin khuur, and also the singing styles like the urtyn duu ("long
song"), and throat-singing (khoomei). The "tsam" is danced to keep away evil spirits and it was seen as reminiscent of
shamanism.
Media
Mongolian press began in 1920 with close ties to the Soviet Union under the Mongolian People's Party, with the
establishment of the Unen ("Truth") newspaper similar to the Soviet <color=#3366CC>Pravda</color>. Until reforms in the 1990s, the government
had strict control of the media and oversaw all publishing, in which no independent media were allowed. The
<color=#3366CC>dissolution of the Soviet Union</color> had a significant impact on Mongolia, where the one-party state grew into a multi-party
democracy, and with that, media freedoms came to the forefront.
According to 2014 Asian Development Bank survey, 80% of Mongolians cited television as their main source of
information. A 1999 law on press freedom, drafted with help from international NGOs, paved the way for media
reforms. The media currently consists of around 300 print and broadcasting outlets. Market reforms have led to an
annually increasing number of people working in the media, along with students at journalism schools. In its 2016
World Press Freedom Index report, <color=#3366CC>Reporters Without Borders</color> classified the media environment as 60th out of 180.
Cuisine
Sports and festivals
The main national festival is Naadam, which has been organized for centuries and takes place over three days in the
summer, consisting of three sports—archery, cross-country horse-racing, and wrestling—traditionally recognized as the
Three Manly Games of Naadam. Naadam is held from 11 to 13 July in the honor of the anniversaries of the National
Democratic Revolution and foundation of the Great Mongol State.
Another popular activity called shagaa is the "flicking" of sheep ankle bones at a target several feet away, using a
flicking motion of the finger to send the small bone flying at targets and trying to knock the target bones off the platform.
At Naadam, this contest is popular among older Mongolians.
Horse riding is especially central to Mongolian culture. The long-distance races that are showcased during Naadam
festivals are one aspect of this, as is the popularity of trick riding. One example of trick riding is the legend that the
Mongolian military hero Damdin Sükhbaatar scattered coins on the ground and then picked them up while riding a
horse at full gallop.
Mongolian wrestling is the most popular sport. It is the highlight of the Three Manly Games of Naadam. Historians claim
that Mongol-style wrestling originated some 7,000 years ago. Hundreds of wrestlers from different cities and aimags
around the country take part in the national wrestling competition. Other sports such as basketball, <color=#3366CC>weightlifting</color>,

<color=#3366CC>powerlifting</color>, association football, athletics, gymnastics, table tennis, <color=#3366CC>jujutsu</color>, <color=#3366CC>karate</color>, <color=#3366CC>aikido</color>, <color=#3366CC>kickboxing</color>, and <color=#3366CC>mixed</color>
<color=#3366CC>martial arts</color> have become popular. <color=#3366CC>Freestyle wrestling</color> has been practiced since 1958. Naidangiin Tüvshinbayar won
Mongolia's first ever Olympic gold medal in the men's 100-kilogram class of judo.
<color=#3366CC>Amateur boxing</color> has been practiced in Mongolia since 1948. The Mongolian Olympic boxing national team was founded
in 1960. Professional boxing began in the 1990s. Mongolia national basketball team enjoyed some success recently,
especially at the East Asian Games. Association football is also played in Mongolia. The Mongolia national football
team began playing national games again during the 1990s; but has not yet qualified for a major international
tournament. The Mongolia Premier League is the top domestic competition.
Several Mongolian women have excelled in <color=#3366CC>pistol shooting</color>: Otryadyn Gündegmaa is a silver medalist of the 2008
Olympic Games, Munkhbayar Dorjsuren is a double world champion and Olympic bronze medal winner (now
representing Germany), while Tsogbadrakhyn Mönkhzul is, as of May 2007, ranked third in the world in the 25-meter
pistol event. Mongolian <color=#3366CC>sumo</color> wrestler <color=#3366CC>Dolgorsürengiin Dagvadorj</color> won 25 top division tournament championships,

<color=#3366CC>Bandy</color> is the only sport in which Mongolia has finished higher than third place at the Asian Winter Games, which
happened in 2011 when the national team captured the silver medal. It led to being chosen as the best Mongolian
sports team of 2011. Mongolia won the bronze medal of the B division at the 2017 Bandy World Championship after
which the then President of Mongolia, Tsakhiagiin Elbegdorj, held a reception for the team.
The Ulaanbaatar Marathon is held annually. Traditional festivals include the Golden Eagle Festival, which draws about
400 eagle hunters on horseback, including the traveler (Mönkhbayart Batsaikhan), to compete with their birds. The Ice

In 2025, a Mongolian team of mixed athletes placed second in the first season of Physical: Asia. Mongolia has built a
strong presence in <color=#3366CC>esports</color>; the most notable team is The MongolZ, which was founded in 2013. The organisation fields
rosters in Counter-Strike 2, <color=#3366CC>Dota 2</color>, Mobile Legends: Bang Bang, PUBG Mobile and <color=#3366CC>Chess</color>, and previously competed in
Valorant. The MongolZ's Counter Strike team has enjoyed numerous international successes, winning the Intel
Extreme Masters Season X Taipei championship in 2016 and, following the team's relaunch in 2023, the 2025 Esports

the Mongolian government as the National Team of Mongolia. The team also became the first Asian team to reach No.
1 in the HLTV World Team Rankings, topping the rankings on 22 and 29 September 2025. The organisation's Chess
team also won the 2026 <color=#3366CC>FIDE</color> World Rapid and Blitz Team Chess Championship in the U2400 category.
In film
The Eagle Huntress is a 2016 internationally co-produced <color=#3366CC>Kazakh-language</color> documentary feature film directed by Otto
Bell that follows the story of Aisholpan Nurgaiv, a 13-year-old Kazakh girl from Mongolia, as she attempts to become
the first female eagle hunter to compete in the eagle festival at Ulgii.
In winter 2023, Australian filmmakers Ben Golotta and Morgan Wright traveled with and filmed two horse herders,
Batbold, aged 18, and Tsagana, aged 22, herding around 2,000 animals across the Tsaikhir Valley, in a traditional
journey to take the horses to safer grazing. The practice is diminishing owing to climate change and young Mongolians
moving to the cities for work. Batbold's father, Bayankhangai, had undertaken ten such grueling trips. The resulting
documentary film, titled Iron Winter, was screened in the Melbourne International Film Festival and the Adelaide Film
Festival.
Tea

Tea is an <color=#3366CC>aromatic</color> <color=#3366CC>beverage</color> prepared by infusion of <color=#3366CC>hot</color> or <color=#3366CC>boiling</color> <color=#3366CC>fresh water</color> with fresh or cured <color=#3366CC>leaves</color> of <color=#3366CC>Camellia</color>

<color=#3366CC>sinensis</color>, an evergreen <color=#3366CC>shrub</color> native to <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color> that originated in the borderlands of <color=#3366CC>southwestern China</color>, <color=#3366CC>northeast</color>
<color=#3366CC>India</color> and northern Myanmar. Tea has a <color=#3366CC>stimulant</color> effect in humans primarily due to its <color=#3366CC>caffeine</color> content.
After plain <color=#3366CC>drinking water</color>, tea is the most widely consumed beverage in the world. There are many varieties of tea
according to differences in <color=#3366CC>cultivars</color>, processing and <color=#3366CC>blends</color>; some have a cooling, slightly bitter and astringent <color=#3366CC>flavor</color>,
while others have taste profiles that include sweet, nutty, floral or grassy notes.
Traditionally, tea is made by steeping loose <color=#3366CC>tea leaves</color> in hot water (usually in a <color=#3366CC>teapot</color> or teacup) for a period of time,
or in the case of compressed and <color=#3366CC>fermented tea</color>, via decoction (<color=#3366CC>simmering</color>) in a <color=#3366CC>kettle</color>. Convenient preparations, such
as tea bag, infuser and press as well as powdered instant tea such as matcha, konacha and <color=#3366CC>chai latte</color>, are also
common. Tea is most commonly consumed as a <color=#3366CC>hot beverage</color> in a plain hot water infusion, although it can also be in
<color=#3366CC>mixed drink</color> forms, such as <color=#3366CC>milk tea</color> and butter tea, sometimes sweetened with added sugar or <color=#3366CC>sugar substitutes</color>, or
alternatively flavored with <color=#3366CC>salt</color> and <color=#3366CC>spices</color>. In modern times, tea can also be served as a cold beverage in the form of
<color=#3366CC>iced tea</color> or in <color=#3366CC>soft drink</color> mixtures such as <color=#3366CC>bubble tea</color>.
Early credible record of <color=#3366CC>tea drinking</color> dates to the 3rd century AD, in a Chinese medical text written by <color=#3366CC>Eastern Han</color>
<color=#3366CC>dynasty</color> physician <color=#3366CC>Hua Tuo</color>. Tea was consumed as a recreational and social beverage during the <color=#3366CC>Tang dynasty</color>, and
Chinese tea culture-inspired <color=#3366CC>ceremonial drinking</color> spread to other <color=#3366CC>Sinospheric</color> countries such as <color=#3366CC>Japan</color> (where it is
known as chado), <color=#3366CC>Korea</color> (known as darye) and <color=#3366CC>Vietnam</color> (typically as part of a wedding ritual). Tea drinking also spread
into Inner Asia and <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color> via the <color=#3366CC>Silk Road</color> and the Tea Horse Road, particularly during the expansion of the
<color=#3366CC>Mongols</color>, for whom the salted milk tea (süütei tsai) has remained part of the <color=#3366CC>staple</color> diet. Outside of the <color=#3366CC>Far East</color>,
Portuguese priests and <color=#3366CC>merchants</color> introduced tea drinking to <color=#3366CC>Europe</color> during the 16th century. During the 17th century,
drinking tea became fashionable in <color=#3366CC>Western Europe</color> as part of the rise of Chinoiserie influence, especially among the
British, who had such a high import demand of tea that they later started to cultivate tea on a large scale in colonial
India and <color=#3366CC>Ceylon</color>, where tea had previously been used only as a <color=#3366CC>herbal medicine</color>.
Etymology
The <color=#3366CC>etymology</color> of the various words for tea reflects the history of transmission of <color=#3366CC>tea drinking</color> and <color=#3366CC>trade</color> from China.
Nearly all of the words for tea worldwide fall into three broad groups: te, cha and chai, present in English as tea, cha or
char, and chai. The earliest of the three to enter English is cha, which came in the 1590s via the <color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color>, who
traded in <color=#3366CC>Macao</color> and picked up the <color=#3366CC>Cantonese</color> pronunciation of the word. The more common tea form arrived in the
17th century via the Dutch, who acquired it via trades from <color=#3366CC>their colonial empire</color> either indirectly from the <color=#3366CC>Malay</color> teh, or
directly from the tê pronunciation in <color=#3366CC>Min Chinese</color>. The third form chai (meaning "spiced tea") originated from a <color=#3366CC>northern</color>

<color=#3366CC>Chinese</color> pronunciation of cha, which travelled via the overland <color=#3366CC>Silk Road</color> to <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Persia</color>, where it picked up
a Persian ending yi. The Chinese word for tea itself was perhaps derived from the non-Sinitic languages of the
botanical homeland of the tea plant in <color=#3366CC>southwest China</color> and northeastern <color=#3366CC>Burma</color> (modern-day <color=#3366CC>Kachin</color> and <color=#3366CC>Shan</color>),
possibly from an archaic <color=#3366CC>Austro-Asiatic</color> root word *la, meaning "leaf".
Origin and history
Botanical origin
Tea plants are native to East Asia and the probable centre of origin of tea is near the source of the <color=#3366CC>Irrawaddy River</color>
from where it spread out fan-wise into southeast China, Indo-China and <color=#3366CC>Assam</color>. The natural home of the tea plant is
considered to be within the comparatively small fan-shaped area between <color=#3366CC>Nagaland</color>, <color=#3366CC>Manipur</color> and <color=#3366CC>Mizoram</color> along the
<color=#3366CC>Burma</color> frontier in the west, through <color=#3366CC>China</color> as far as the <color=#3366CC>Zhejiang</color> Province in the east, and from this line generally south
through the hills to Burma and <color=#3366CC>Thailand</color> to <color=#3366CC>Vietnam</color>. The west–east axis indicated above is about 2,400 km long
extending from longitude 95°-120°E. The north–south axis covers about 1,920 km, starting from the northern part of
Burma, latitude 29°N passing through <color=#3366CC>Yunnan</color>, Tongkin, Thailand, <color=#3366CC>Laos</color> and on to Annan, reaching latitude 11°N.
Chinese (small-leaf) type tea (C. sinensis var. sinensis) may have originated in southern China possibly with
hybridization of unknown wild tea relatives. Since there are no known wild populations of this tea, its origin is
speculative.
Given their genetic differences forming distinct <color=#3366CC>clades</color>, Chinese Assam-type tea (C. sinensis var. assamica) may have
two parentages – one being found in southern <color=#3366CC>Yunnan</color> (Xishuangbanna, Pu'er City) and the other in western Yunnan
(Lincang, Baoshan). Many types of Southern Yunnan Assam tea have been hybridized with the closely related species
Camellia taliensis. Unlike Southern Yunnan Assam tea, Western Yunnan Assam tea shares many genetic similarities
with Indian Assam-type tea (also C. sinensis var. assamica). Thus, Western Yunnan Assam tea and Indian Assam tea
both may have originated from the same parent plant in the area where southwestern China, Indo-Burma, and Tibet
meet. However, as the Indian Assam tea shares no haplotypes with Western Yunnan Assam tea, Indian Assam tea is
likely to have originated from an independent domestication. Some Indian Assam tea appears to have hybridized with
the species Camellia pubicosta.
Assuming a generation of 12 years, Chinese small-leaf tea is estimated to have diverged from Assam tea around
22,000 years ago, while Chinese Assam tea and Indian Assam tea diverged 2,800 years ago. The divergence of
Chinese small-leaf tea and Assam tea would correspond to the last <color=#3366CC>glacial maximum</color>.
Early tea drinking
People in ancient East Asia ate tea for centuries, perhaps even <color=#3366CC>millennia</color>, before ever consuming it as a beverage.
They would nibble on the leaves raw, add them to <color=#3366CC>soups</color> or <color=#3366CC>greens</color>, or <color=#3366CC>ferment</color> them and chew them as areca nut is
<color=#3366CC>chewed</color>.
Tea drinking may have begun in the region of <color=#3366CC>Yunnan</color>, where it was used for medicinal purposes. It is believed that in
<color=#3366CC>Sichuan</color>, "people began to boil tea leaves for consumption into a concentrated liquid without the addition of other
leaves or herbs, thereby using tea as a bitter yet stimulating drink, rather than as a medicinal concoction."
Chinese legends attribute the invention of tea to the mythical <color=#3366CC>Shennong</color> (in central and northern China) in 2737 BC,
although evidence suggests that tea drinking may have been introduced from southwest China. The earliest written
records of tea come from China. The word tú appears in the <color=#3366CC>Shijing</color> and other ancient texts to signify a kind of "bitter
vegetable", and it is possible that it referred to many different plants such as sow thistle, <color=#3366CC>chicory</color>, or smartweed, as well
as tea. In the Chronicles of Huayang, it was recorded that the Ba people in Sichuan presented tu to the <color=#3366CC>Zhou</color> king. The
<color=#3366CC>Qin</color> later conquered the state of Ba and its neighbour Shu, and according to the 17th-century scholar Gu Yanwu who
wrote in Ri Zhi Lu: "It was after the Qin had taken Shu that they learned how to drink tea." Another possible early
reference to tea is found in a letter written by the <color=#3366CC>Qin dynasty</color> general Liu Kun who requested that some "real tea" to be
sent to him.
The earliest known physical evidence of tea was discovered in 2016 in the mausoleum of Emperor Jing of Han in <color=#3366CC>Xi'an</color>,
indicating that tea from the genus Camellia was drunk by <color=#3366CC>Han dynasty</color> emperors as early as the second century BC.
The Han dynasty work "The Contract for a Youth", written by Wang Bao in 59 BC, contains the first known reference to
boiling tea. Among the tasks listed to be undertaken by the youth, the contract states that "he shall boil tea and fill the
utensils" and "he shall buy tea at Wuyang". The first record of tea cultivation is dated to this period, during which tea
was cultivated on Meng Mountain near <color=#3366CC>Chengdu</color>. Another early credible record of tea drinking dates to the 3rd century
AD, in a medical text by the Chinese physician <color=#3366CC>Hua Tuo</color>, who stated, "to drink bitter t'u constantly makes one think
better." However, before the <color=#3366CC>Tang dynasty</color>, tea-drinking was primarily a southern Chinese practice centered in
Jiankang. Tea was disdained by the <color=#3366CC>Northern dynasties</color> aristocrats, who describe it as inferior to yogurt. It became
widely consumed during the Tang dynasty, when it spread to Korea, <color=#3366CC>Japan</color>, and Vietnam. The Classic of Tea, a treatise
on tea and its preparations, was written by the 8th century Chinese writer, Lu Yu. The current Chinese word for tea
appeared in The Classic of Tea by removing a stroke from the word tu. Lu was known to have influenced tea drinking
on a large part in China.
Developments
Through the centuries, a variety of techniques for processing tea, and a number of different forms of tea, were
developed. During the Han and Six Dynasties, tea was steamed and pounded, shaped into cake form, slowly dried over
low fire, and suspended to air dry. Chunks of tea were then boiled to drink, flavoured with orange peels, <color=#3366CC>jujube</color>, mint,
ginger or <color=#3366CC>scallion</color>. Tea was similarly prepared in cake form during the Tang dynasty, but Lu Yu disparaged the use of
various condiments to flavour the tea apart from salt. By the <color=#3366CC>Song dynasty</color>, loose-leaf tea was developed and became
common. During the <color=#3366CC>Yuan</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ming</color> dynasties, unoxidized tea leaves were first stirred in a hot dry pan, then rolled and
air-dried, a process that stops the <color=#3366CC>oxidation</color> process that would have turned the leaves dark, thereby allowing tea to
remain green. In the 15th century, <color=#3366CC>oolong</color> tea, in which the leaves are allowed to partially oxidize before being heated in
the pan, was developed. Western tastes, however, favoured the fully oxidized <color=#3366CC>black tea</color>, and the leaves were allowed to
oxidize further. <color=#3366CC>Yellow tea</color> was an accidental discovery in the production of green tea during the Ming dynasty, when
apparently careless practices allowed the leaves to turn yellow, which yielded a different flavour.
Worldwide spread
Tea was first introduced to Western priests and merchants in China during the 16th century, at which time it was
termed chá. The earliest European reference to tea, written as chiai, came from Delle navigationi e viaggi written by
Venetian Giambattista Ramusio in 1545. The first recorded shipment of tea by a European nation was in 1607 when
the Dutch East India Company moved a cargo of tea from <color=#3366CC>Macao</color> to Java, then two years later, the Dutch bought the
first assignment of tea which was from Hirado in Japan to be shipped to Europe. Tea became a fashionable drink in

<color=#3366CC>The Hague</color> in the Netherlands, and the Dutch introduced the drink to <color=#3366CC>Germany</color>, <color=#3366CC>France</color>, and across the Atlantic to <color=#3366CC>New</color>
<color=#3366CC>Amsterdam</color> (New York).
In 1567, Russian people came in contact with tea when <color=#3366CC>Cossack</color> leaders (atamans) Petrov and Yalyshev visited China.
The Mongolian Khan donated to <color=#3366CC>Tsar</color> <color=#3366CC>Michael I</color> four poods (65–70 kg) of tea in 1638. According to Jeremiah Curtin, it
was possibly in 1636 that Vassili Starkov was sent as envoy to the Altyn Khan. He was given 250 pounds of tea as a
gift to the tsar. Starkov at first refused, seeing no use for a load of dead leaves, but the Khan insisted. Thus was tea
introduced to Russia. In 1679, Russia concluded a treaty on regular tea supplies from China via camel caravan in
exchange for furs. It is today considered the de facto national beverage.
The first record of tea in English came from a letter written by Richard Wickham, who ran an <color=#3366CC>East India Company</color> office
in Japan, writing to a merchant in Macao requesting "the best sort of chaw" in 1615. Peter Mundy, a traveller and
merchant who came across tea in <color=#3366CC>Fujian</color> in 1637, wrote, "chaa – only water with a kind of herb boyled in it". Tea was
sold in a coffee house in London in 1657, <color=#3366CC>Samuel Pepys</color> tasted tea in 1660, and Catherine of Braganza took the
tea-drinking habit to the English court when she married <color=#3366CC>Charles II</color> in 1662. Tea, however, was not widely consumed in
the British Isles until the 18th century and remained expensive until the latter part of that period. English drinkers
preferred to add sugar and milk to black tea, as the tea of choice in the 1720s. Tea smuggling during the 18th century
led to the general public being able to afford and consume tea. The British government removed the tax on tea, thereby
eliminating the smuggling trade, by 1785. In Britain and Ireland, tea was initially consumed as a luxury item on special
occasions, such as religious festivals, wakes, and domestic work gatherings. The price of tea in Europe fell steadily
during the 19th century, especially after Indian tea began to arrive in large quantities; by the late 19th century tea had
become an everyday beverage for all levels of society. Consuming tea played a role in historical events – the Tea Act
of 1773 provoked the <color=#3366CC>Boston Tea Party</color> that escalated into the <color=#3366CC>American Revolution</color>. The need to address the issue of
British trade deficit because of the trade in tea resulted in the Opium Wars. The Qing <color=#3366CC>Kangxi Emperor</color> had banned
foreign products from being sold in China, decreeing in 1685 that all goods bought from China must be paid for in silver
coin or bullion. Traders from other nations then sought to find another product, in this case opium, to sell to China to
earn back the silver they were required to pay for tea and other commodities. The subsequent attempts by the Chinese
Government to curtail the trade in opium led to war.
Chinese small-leaf-type tea was introduced into India in 1836 by the British in an attempt to break the Chinese
monopoly on tea. In 1841, Archibald Campbell brought seeds of Chinese tea from the Kumaun region and
experimented with planting tea in <color=#3366CC>Darjeeling</color>. The Alubari tea garden was opened in 1856, and Darjeeling tea began to
be produced. In 1848, Robert Fortune was sent by the <color=#3366CC>East India Company</color> on a mission to China to bring the tea plant
back to Great Britain. He began his journey in high secrecy as his mission occurred in the lull between the <color=#3366CC>First Opium</color>
<color=#3366CC>War</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Second Opium War</color>. The Chinese tea plants he brought back were introduced to the <color=#3366CC>Himalayas</color>, though
most did not survive. The British had discovered that a different variety of tea was endemic to <color=#3366CC>Assam</color> and the northeast
region of India, which was then hybridized with Chinese small-leaf-type tea. Using Chinese planting and cultivation
techniques, the British colonial government established a tea industry by offering land in Assam to any European who
agreed to cultivate it for export. Tea was originally consumed only by Anglo-Indians; however, it became widely
consumed in India in the 1950s because of a successful advertising campaign by the India Tea Board. The British
introduced tea industry to Sri Lanka (then Ceylon) in 1867.
Chemical composition
Physically speaking, tea has properties of both a <color=#3366CC>solution</color> and a <color=#3366CC>suspension</color>. It is a solution of the water-soluble
compounds extracted from the tea leaves, such as the polyphenols and amino acids. Tea infusions are among most
consumed beverages globally.
<color=#3366CC>Caffeine</color> makes up about 3% of tea's dry weight, which translates to between 30 and 90 milligrams per 250 mL cup
depending on the type, brand, and brewing method. A study found that the caffeine content of one gram of black tea
ranged from 22 to 28 mg, while the caffeine content of one gram of green tea ranged from 11 to 20 mg, reflecting a
significant difference. Tea contains small amounts of <color=#3366CC>theobromine</color> and <color=#3366CC>theophylline</color>, which are <color=#3366CC>xanthines</color> and
<color=#3366CC>stimulants</color>, similar to caffeine.
The astringency in tea can be attributed to the presence of <color=#3366CC>polyphenols</color>. These are the most abundant compounds in
tea leaves, making up 30–40% of their composition. Polyphenols in tea include <color=#3366CC>flavonoids</color>, epigallocatechin gallate, and
other catechins.
Health effects
There is no high-quality evidence showing that tea consumption has health effects, other than possibly increasing
alertness caused by <color=#3366CC>caffeine</color> in the leaves. There is insufficient evidence that tea polyphenols have any effect on health
or lowering disease risk.
Black and green teas contain no <color=#3366CC>essential nutrients</color> in significant amounts, with the exception of the <color=#3366CC>dietary mineral</color>
<color=#3366CC>manganese</color>, at 0.5 mg per cup or 26% of the Reference Daily Intake. <color=#3366CC>Fluoride</color> is sometimes present in tea; certain
types of "brick tea", made from old leaves and stems, have the highest levels, enough to pose a health risk if too much
tea is drunk, which has been attributed to high levels of fluoride in soils, acidic soils, and long brewing.
Cultivation and harvesting
Camellia sinensis is an evergreen plant that grows mainly in <color=#3366CC>tropical</color> and <color=#3366CC>subtropical</color> climates. Some varieties can
tolerate oceanic climates and are cultivated as far north as <color=#3366CC>Cornwall</color> in England, Perthshire in Scotland, <color=#3366CC>Washington</color> in
the United States, and <color=#3366CC>Vancouver Island</color> in Canada. In the Southern Hemisphere, tea is grown as far south as <color=#3366CC>Hobart</color>
in Tasmania and <color=#3366CC>Waikato</color> in New Zealand.
Tea plants are propagated from seed and cuttings; about 4 to 12 years are needed for a plant to bear seed and about
three years before a new plant is ready for harvesting. In addition to a <color=#3366CC>zone 8</color> climate or warmer, tea plants require at
least 1200 mm of rainfall per year and prefer <color=#3366CC>acidic soils</color>. Many high-quality tea plants are cultivated at elevations of up
to 2000 m above sea level. Though at these heights the plants grow more slowly, they acquire a better flavour.
Two principal varieties are used: Camellia sinensis var. sinensis, which is used for most Chinese, Formosan and
Japanese teas, and C. sinensis var. assamica, used in Pu-erh and most Indian teas (but not Darjeeling). Within these
botanical varieties, many strains and modern clonal varieties are known. Leaf size is the chief criterion for the
classification of tea plants, with three primary classifications being: Assam type, characterised by the largest leaves;
China type, characterised by the smallest leaves; and Cambodian type, characterised by leaves of intermediate size.
The Cambodian-type tea (C. assamica subsp. lasiocaly) was originally considered a type of Assam tea. However, later
genetic work showed that it is a hybrid between Chinese small-leaf tea and Assam-type large-leaf tea. Darjeeling tea
appears to be another hybrid of the same sort.
A tea plant will grow into a tree of up to 16 m if left undisturbed, but cultivated plants are generally pruned to waist
height for ease of harvesting. The short plants also bear more new shoots which provide new and tender leaves and
